extracted.intended_audience: educated British readers concerned with the moral and political effects of the French Revolution (late 18th-century public/intelligentsia)
extracted.subtask_description: A moral and political essay arguing against the 'Illumination' (revolutionary/Illuminati) tendencies of the French Revolution and defending religion, social order, and the proper cultivation and role of women in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know God only by his attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Therefore we know God only by his attributes. What are these? The wise and excellent contrivance, structure, and final aim of all things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that humans cannot know God's nature directly (we have notions of attributes only); knowledge of God is inferred from the contrivance and final aims of creation. The passage links this epistemology to worship (we worship a governing God) and rejects pantheistic or impersonal conceptions that lack providence.

rubrics_metrics.name: God must be a governing Being (not mere perfection)
rubrics_metrics.description: “But a being, however perfect, without government, is not God; for we say, my God... We cannot say my eternal, my infinite.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that divine perfection without dominion/providence would be equivalent to Fate and would not command reverence, hope, love, or fear; therefore genuine deity includes governance and final aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific discovery humbles yet enriches human dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Passage summarised from Delaplace: scientific labour shows us 'an insignificant planet' yet 'the sublime discoveries we have made richly repay this humble situation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science reduces anthropocentric pride (we are on an insignificant planet) but still provides intellectual delight and titles to intelligence; humility before cosmic scale is compatible with admiration for human reason and discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal induction: nature accomplishes her plans
rubrics_metrics.description: “...that nature accomplishes all her plans, and that every class of beings attains all the improvement of which it is capable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a probabilistic argument for an afterlife: if natural improvement is the norm, human intellect should be capable of further improvement beyond this life. This functions as a principle of expectation in moral/philosophical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion (Gospel) supplies consolation and moral simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: “They think it worthy of the Father of mankind, and they receive it with thankful hearts, admiring above all things the simplicity of its morality... 'Do to another what you can reasonably wish that another should do to you.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions the Christian Gospel as offering simple, comprehensible moral rules and consolation to the modest/humble; contrasts it with systems that promise felicity in this life and with abstract philosophies (e.g., Stoicism) that may not support most people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoicism insufficient for the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: “They grant that the Stoics were persons of noble and exalted minds... but they confess that they themselves do not feel all that support from Stoical principles which man too frequently needs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that Stoic self-sufficiency and heroic fortitude are rare; most people require religion's emotional and moral supports. Stoical satisfaction is a small minority's remedy, not generalisable to masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware superstition and priestly corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: “...there have been enthusiasts, or villains, who have taken advantage of this... cheats, who have misrepresented God to mankind, have filled us with vain terrors, and have then quieted our fears by fines, and sacrifices, and mortifications..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes legitimate religion (moral instruction, consolation) from corrupt forms that exploit fears for power and wealth; warns that such corruption distorts true religion and public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illumination/revolutionary doctrines undermine moral and social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated denunciation of 'Illumination' and the Illuminati: their proposals 'destroy the grounds of morality' and will lead to vice prevailing and social desolation (with France used as example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that attempts to overturn established social constitutions in pursuit of utopian felicity permit wicked means, erode moral restraints, and cause immediate suffering (executions, spoliations). The text uses contemporary French events as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women are central ornaments and moral guardians of society
rubrics_metrics.description: “Then let us reflect that it is woman that is to grace the whole... it is the very constitution of man, that woman, and every thing connected with woman, must appear as the ornament of life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that women's social role as moral ornaments and domestic guardians is natural and indispensable for rearing and civilising men; warns that corrupting women harms the whole social fabric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect women from revolutionary/immoral corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nothing in the whole constitution of the Illuminati that strikes me with more horror than the proposals... to enlist the women in this shocking warfare... If any of my countrywomen shall honour these pages... I would call on them... to join against these enemies of human nature and profligate degraders of the sex."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit exhortation aimed at women to resist participation in Illuminated/revolutionary movements that the author believes will degrade the sex and reduce their dignity and social standing; frames it as a duty to save society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement and luxury foster pursuit of perceptible pleasure and moral decay
rubrics_metrics.description: “Man is immersed in luxury. Our accommodations are now so numerous that every thing is pleasure... This discontent with the natural condition of things, and this disposition to refinement, is a characteristic of our species..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observes that increased comforts lead to refined tastes and a general chase for perceptible pleasure, which can displace moral priorities and make society more susceptible to decadence and vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female modesty and natural moral sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The author cites Ledyard: women are 'civil, obliging, tender, and humane... ever inclined to be gay and cheerful, timorous and modest; and that they do not hesitate... to perform a kind or generous action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses cross-cultural travel testimony to characterise female virtues as widespread and robust; this is used both to praise women and to argue that revolutionary attempts misjudge or misrepresent female dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cultivate women's intellects is culpable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Are we not guilty in some degree, when we do not cultivate in the women those powers of mind, and those dispositions of heart, which would equally dignify them in every station... I cannot think that we do this."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that society has a responsibility to cultivate women's minds and virtues; neglecting this is blameworthy and contributes to social problems. The author links proper cultivation with prevention of degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public art and revived classical fashions can be used to erode modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of French trends: 'Madame Tallien... presenting themselves to the public view, with bared limbs, à la Sauvage' and Grecian/Amazon/à la Grecque fashions are blamed for promoting dissoluteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that adoption of certain fashions, theatre spectacles, and public displays (including classical nudity and gymnastic shows) will accelerate moral decay and weaken familial and social bonds; treats artistic contagion as politically and morally consequential.
